t: #3875 Construct Uniform Parity Array I — Parity Case Analysis
o: Each output element is either the original value or a difference of two distinct original values; we need all outputs to share one parity. Modulo 2, subtraction equals addition, so nums1[i]-nums1[j] has parity parity(i)+parity(j). An even element can only become odd if some other element is odd; an odd element can never become even unless another odd exists (odd-odd = even). Checking the examples: [2,3] mixes parities, so making everything odd works (2-3=-1, keep 3); [4,6] is all even, so keeping both works. In fact a short case analysis shows the answer is always true: all-even works if there are no odds, all-odd works if there are no evens, and a mix supports all-odd (each even pairs with an odd, each odd stays).
k: Modulo 2, a difference x-y has parity equal to x+y, so only parities of inputs matter.
All-even is possible iff there is no odd element; all-odd is possible iff there is no even element, or an odd exists to pair with each even.
Combining the cases (all even / all odd / mixed) shows a valid construction always exists, so the answer is constantly true.

a.i: Count odd elements. If all elements share one parity, keep them all. Otherwise the array is mixed and the all-odd construction works: every odd element is kept, every even element subtracts some odd element. Hence we can simply verify the reasoning and return true.
s: Count how many elements are odd.
If countOdd == 0 (all even) or countEven == 0 (all odd), return true (keep everything).
Otherwise (mixed), return true using the all-odd construction — every even element pairs with an existing odd.

a.n: Approach 2: Try Each Target Parity with Pair Search
a.i: Instead of reasoning globally, attempt each target parity p in {even, odd}: element i is satisfiable under p if it already has parity p, or some j != i satisfies (nums1[i] + nums1[j]) % 2 == p. If either parity is universally satisfiable, return true. This generalizes easily if the operation set changes.
s: For p = 0 and p = 1, check every index i.
Index i passes if nums1[i] % 2 == p, or any other element j makes (nums1[i]+nums1[j]) % 2 == p.
Return true if all indices pass for either p; otherwise false.
a.t: O(n^2) — for each element we scan for a suitable partner.

w: Lead with the O(n) case analysis; the pairwise version is a good sanity check and generalizes better. Pitfall: forgetting n = 1 (trivially true, only the identity choice exists) and forgetting that subtraction mod 2 behaves like addition. Likely follow-up: what if the allowed operations were x+y or x*y instead — redo the parity algebra accordingly.
